classical_method: All three families are Kalshi markets recorded by the same collector: order-book deltas, snapshots and trades. For each market-day I rebuilt the top-5 book on both sides after every event. For binaries the NO bids are mapped to YES asks, so every market is on one bid/ask grid. Windows are the last N book events (N = 16, 64, 256, 1024) or the last W seconds (1, 10, 60, 600 s). Every feature is a ratio, share, correlation or normalised quantity: shares of event types, inter-event-time shape after dividing by its own mean, spread relative to realised volatility, depth shares by level, autocorrelations, impact per trade. A separate trivial group (event rate, absolute depth, price level/bound, relative tick size) is computed but kept out of every model unless a row says otherwise.
classify_method: LightGBM multiclass with class-balanced weights; at most 20,000 windows per market class. The split is by market-day (hash of ticker and date), so no market appears in both train and test. Non-trivial = all features except the trivial group. Strict additionally drops the seven features whose value depends on the price grid (spread in ticks, share of one-tick spreads, spread dispersion, level gaps, mid-jump size, deep and inside-spread add shares). Balanced accuracy is the mean per-class recall, so chance is 1/number of classes.
ae_method: Each sample is the last 64 events before an anchor. Every event is a 16-number token: event type, side, add or cancel, distance from the touch in ticks, size relative to the sequence's own mean touch depth, log inter-arrival time standardised within the sequence, spread, L1 imbalance, mid change, and depth shares. No absolute size or activity level survives this normalisation. The autoencoder is a 2-layer GRU encoder → 16-d bottleneck → GRU decoder that reconstructs the whole sequence (MSE). It is trained without labels on a class-balanced sample. Probes (logistic regression and GBM) then try to read the market type from the 16 numbers. The strict variant zeroes the three tick-denominated token fields.
trades_method: A taker order is all fills with the same exchange millisecond and side. Features are taken from the book before the order's own deltas arrive (the exchange sends the depletion before the trade message). Order features: size relative to depth at the touch and to the recent median order, levels walked, time since the previous order relative to its recent median, run of same-side orders, prior 1/10/60 s move in the order's direction, signed imbalance, spread, distance to the 0/1 bound, fee in ticks. Labels at 0.1, 0.5, 1 and 10 s: toxic = the mid ends past the fill price in the taker's direction (the maker lost even after the spread); net>0 = buy at the fill, sell at the touch at t+h, pay two taker fees (Kalshi 0.07·P·(1−P) per contract per side; perps assumed 2 bp per side, which is an assumption to check). Inputs are compared in five sets, from order-only up to order + window features + AE embedding + classifier activations. One multi-task MLP predicts all 12 targets at once.
fair_method: BTC 15-minute markets; train on Sep 18–21, validate on Sep 22, test on Sep 23 (new markets, new day). Targets are mid changes in ticks at 0.1, 0.5, 1 and 10 s. The raw model input is the last 128 events: type, side, add/cancel, price offset from the current mid in ticks, log size, and each event's age in seconds. Time is encoded with fixed log-spaced sinusoids (periods 1 ms – 1000 s) plus a learned Time2Vec term, instead of a token-position encoding. A book-state token (top-5 sizes and offsets) and a readout token are prepended. The GRU reads the same tokens in time order with log inter-arrival gaps added. Baselines (ridge, LightGBM, MLP) use the handcrafted window features at the same anchors.
fair_arch:
Training curves for every run, including the continued Transformer, are on the Training curves page.

Architecture

Tokens. One token per book event: a learned type embedding (delta / trade / snapshot), a learned embedding of the price offset from the current mid rounded to ticks (−50…50), and a linear map of side, add/cancel, scaled offset and standardised log size. Time. Each token gets the encoding of its age (seconds before the prediction time): sin/cos at 16 log-spaced periods from 1 ms to 1,000 s, plus log-age, a same-millisecond flag and a learned Time2Vec term. There is no positional index, so two events 3 ms apart look different from two events 3 s apart. Transformer: [readout] + [book-state token: top-5 sizes and offsets] + 128 events → 4 pre-norm layers, d=96, 4 heads → 4 outputs. GRU: same tokens in time order plus a log inter-arrival embedding → 2-layer GRU (160) → concatenated with the book-state embedding → 4 outputs. Both are trained with MSE on targets standardised per horizon, AdamW with warm-up and linear decay, and time-boxed.
classical: Yes, crypto and sports books behave differently even after removing volume, price level and tick size. The biggest raw separator is event rate (BTC 15m vs sports d = 3.6), which is exactly the trivial difference we exclude; many differences remain without it.

Timing. Crypto binaries and perps update in bursts: 68% of BTC 15m events and 63–78% of perp events arrive within 1 ms of the previous one, against 26–41% for sports. After dividing by each market's own mean gap, sports inter-arrival times are more irregular (CV 2.8–3.9 vs 2.3 for BTC 15m).

The BTC 15m book churns without moving. Only 0.4% of its book events change the mid, against 6–16% in sports and 5–8% in perps. Its spread is one tick almost all the time, and it is wide relative to how far the mid actually travels (spread/volatility well above the sports median).
Where liquidity sits. The touch holds 27% of top-5 depth in BTC 15m and 29% in MLB, but only 4–10% in perps, whose liquidity sits a few levels back.

Order-book imbalance predicts the next second in crypto and perps, not in sports. Going from imbalance −0.9 to +0.9 shifts the expected 1 s mid move from −0.42 to +0.42 ticks in crypto and from −1.4 to +1.6 ticks in perps. In sports the curve is flat (within ±0.08 ticks): sports prices move on game events, not on queue pressure.

Shared behaviour. Trade signs are persistent everywhere (lag-1 autocorrelation 0.45–0.65), which is consistent with order splitting, and the mid bounces everywhere (negative lag-1 autocorrelation of mid changes).

Sports taker flow is mostly benign; perp flow is close to a coin flip. One second after a taker order the mid has moved past the fill price for 12–17% of sports orders, 26% of BTC 15m orders, 27–37% of other crypto binaries and about 47% of perp orders. After two taker fees and the exit spread, 21% of BTC 15m round trips are profitable at 10 s, against 3–5% in sports.

The most toxic orders are the ones that exactly clear the touch (size ≈ displayed depth): 59% toxic in crypto, 65% in perps and 43% in sports, against 3–19% for small orders. Orders that follow a move of more than 3 ticks in the prior 10 s in their own direction are also more toxic (sports 30% vs 10% when the price was flat).
overview: Is crypto structure different from sports? Yes, decisively. With features that ignore volume, price level and tick size, a classifier tells crypto binaries, sports and perps apart with 0.91 balanced accuracy from 16 book events and 0.99 from 1,024. BTC 15m vs sports is ~100%.

Does structure differ market to market? Yes. 13 market types are told apart with 0.86 balanced accuracy (chance 0.08). Crypto products and perps are each nearly perfectly separable; sports leagues are distinct but more similar to each other (0.78 within sports).

What differs: crypto and perps trade in millisecond bursts and their book imbalance predicts the next second; sports books update more irregularly, imbalance carries almost no information, and taker flow is much less toxic (12–17% of orders see the price run past the fill within 1 s, vs 26% in BTC 15m and ~47% in perps).

Can the next taker order be judged? Yes for toxicity: AUC 0.93 (0.1 s) to 0.79 (10 s) on unseen markets, and 0.77–0.92 within each family at 1 s. Large orders that clear the touch after a move in their direction are the toxic ones. The autoencoder and classifier embeddings add nothing beyond the order and window features. Even the model's best 1% of predicted-profitable taker trades still lose money after two fees.

Bitter lesson: raw events win, and more compute keeps helping. A GRU over the last 128 raw book events (each event's age encoded in continuous time) beats handcrafted-feature LightGBM at every horizon on a held-out day. BTC 15m: R² 0.262 / 0.164 / 0.123 / 0.018 (60-min run) vs 0.232 / 0.152 / 0.114 / 0.015. BTC perp: 0.187 / 0.078 / 0.046 / 0.005 vs 0.128 / 0.044 / 0.023 / −0.002. The Transformer ties or slightly beats LightGBM; on CPU it gets about a third of the GRU's training steps.
Part 3: the collector VM has been recording BTC (and all other) Kalshi markets since 08:30 UTC; the data is in the tape under dt=2026-11-17.
classify: Market family is almost perfectly identifiable from scale-free book behaviour. Crypto binaries, sports and perps are separated with 0.906 balanced accuracy from just the last 16 events and 0.986 from the last 1,024, using the strict set (no volume, rate, depth level, price level or any tick-size-dependent quantity). Chance is 0.33.

Individual markets are also distinct. Over 13 fine classes (chance 0.08), strict features reach 0.68 (16 events), 0.75 (64), 0.81 (256) and 0.86 (1,024). Clock windows behave the same way: 0.72 with 1 s of history up to 0.87 with 10 minutes. More history always helps, and there is no plateau yet at 1,024 events.
BTC 15m vs sports is essentially perfect (0.995 with 16 events, 1.000 with 256). BTC 15m is the most distinctive market: 100% recall in the confusion matrix.

Where the confusion is: almost entirely within sports (NFL↔NCAAF 12–14%, otherwise spread evenly across sports). Within crypto the products separate at 0.99; within perps at 0.97 (BTC perp is sometimes taken for ETH or alt perps). Sports-only classification reaches 0.78 against a 0.17 chance rate, so sports leagues still have their own signature, just a weaker one.

It is not one magic feature. Removing imbalance costs 1.8 points, spread 1.8, imbalance and spread together 3.8, timing 5.4 (the largest), depth 2.2. Each group on its own is far weaker than all together (timing alone 0.52, depth alone 0.58, imbalance alone 0.37). The top individual features are batching (share of events within 1 ms), spread of log inter-arrival times, trade-size dispersion, level gaps and depth shape.

Sanity check on trivial features: rate, absolute depth, price level and relative tick on their own give 0.90 coarse / 0.62 fine. Adding them to the non-trivial set only moves fine accuracy from 0.84 to 0.88. The structural result does not depend on them.
ae: An embedding learned without labels already separates the families. A 16-number summary of the last 64 events (reconstruction MSE 0.49 vs 1.29 for predicting the mean) lets a GBM probe recover crypto / sports / perp with 0.83 balanced accuracy (linear probe 0.78; chance 0.33).

It keeps much less of the fine-grained identity. 13-class accuracy from the embedding is 0.54 (linear 0.45; chance 0.08), while a supervised GRU on the same 64-event input reaches 0.85. The autoencoder spends its capacity on what varies most event to event (spread, imbalance, where the next order lands), not on what distinguishes leagues.

Per market: BTC 15m (88% recall), alt perps (89%), ETH perp (80%) and alt 15m (79%) stay distinct in the embedding. The sports leagues mostly collapse into one cloud (16–49% recall, confused with one another), so at the 64-event scale sports books look alike.

What the dimensions mean (by correlation with the handcrafted features): z1 and z0 are spread and one-tick-ness against touch depth relative to trade size; z8 and z14 are L1 imbalance; z12 is deep vs at-touch activity; z11 and z15 are order size relative to touch depth. BTC 15m sits at the tight-spread, deep-touch-relative-to-trades end (z1 −1.2, z15 −1.0); perps at the opposite end with most activity away from the touch (z12 +1.0, z15 +1.4).

Strict autoencoder (distance-from-touch, spread and mid-change fields blanked, so no tick-size information): probes still recover family at 0.77 (GBM) / 0.69 (linear) and the 13 markets at 0.40 / 0.27 (chance 0.33 / 0.08). Removing tick information costs about 0.07 coarse and 0.13 fine, so most, but not all, of the embedding's signal is behavioural.
trades: Yes: the book state plus the incoming order predicts whether that order is toxic. On 235k held-out taker orders from unseen markets, ROC-AUC for “the mid ends past the fill price” is 0.93 / 0.89 / 0.87 / 0.79 at 0.1 / 0.5 / 1 / 10 s (LightGBM; the multi-task MLP is 0.92 / 0.88 / 0.86 / 0.78). The confusion matrices at a validation-chosen threshold give balanced accuracy 0.84 / 0.80 / 0.78 / 0.71. For example at 1 s, 82% of toxic orders are flagged while 74% of benign ones are correctly passed.

It is not just the market family's base rate. AUC within one family at 1 s: sports 0.92 (base rate 14%), crypto binaries 0.82 (31%), perps 0.77 (47%). Per market at 1 s: tennis 0.95, NFL 0.93, MLB 0.92, hourly crypto 0.87, BTC 15m 0.77, alt 15m 0.76, BTC perp 0.68, ETH perp 0.56. Sports flow is the easiest to classify; BTC and ETH perps are the hardest.

The order itself carries most of the signal. Order-only features already give 0.91 / 0.88 / 0.85 / 0.77. Adding the window microstructure features adds about 0.01 AUC at every horizon. The autoencoder embedding and the classifier activations add nothing on top (0.917 vs 0.918). Used instead of the handcrafted window they recover almost all of its value (0.915), so they encode the same information. Top features: order size relative to depth at the touch (by far), market family, inter-arrival irregularity, how far the order walked the book, price paid vs mid, prior 1 s move, fee.

What a toxic order looks like. The classic pattern shows up clearly. Orders sized to exactly clear the touch (size ≈ displayed depth) are 43–60% toxic depending on the prior move, against 2–20% for small orders. Within every size bucket, toxicity rises when the order chases a prior 10 s move of more than 2 ticks in its own direction (e.g. 60% vs 43% for touch-clearing orders). So a large order after a move is usually informed, which matches the hypothesis. Part of the short-horizon effect is mechanical (clearing the touch moves the mid), so the 1 s and 10 s numbers are the honest measure of information.

Profitable after two taker fees: predictable, but still not profitable. AUC for “round trip clears fees + exit spread” is 0.91 / 0.88 / 0.87 / 0.82. The base rate is tiny (1.6% at 0.1 s, 12% at 10 s). In the model's top 1% the hit rate rises to 29% / 35% / 38% / 61%, but the average net PnL of those trades is still negative (−5.5 / −2.7 / −2.6 / −0.7 ticks). Following the flow as a taker does not pay; this information is more useful for avoiding toxic flow as a maker (quote widening / skew) than for taking.
Markout regression (in spread units): R² 0.57 / 0.45 / 0.38 / 0.13, mostly from the predictable half-spread-plus-impact component.
fair: The bitter-lesson result holds: a model reading raw events matches or beats hand-engineered features, and the margin is largest where the handcrafted features were weakest.

BTC 15m (held-out day Sep 23, unseen markets). GRU on the last 128 raw events: R² 0.251 / 0.158 / 0.119 / 0.018 at 0.1 / 0.5 / 1 / 10 s. Handcrafted LightGBM: 0.232 / 0.152 / 0.114 / 0.015; handcrafted MLP: 0.234 / 0.148 / 0.113 / 0.014. The Transformer ties LightGBM after 40 minutes (0.231 / 0.152 / 0.115 / 0.015) and edges past it after 75 minutes (0.233 / 0.154 / 0.116 / 0.018).

BTC perp, where the handcrafted features were built for binaries and transfer poorly: GRU 0.187 / 0.078 / 0.046 / 0.005 vs LightGBM 0.128 / 0.044 / 0.023 / −0.002, i.e. +47% at 0.1 s and roughly double at 0.5–1 s. The Transformer (only 1,300 steps in 25 min) roughly matches LightGBM.
When the mid does move, both sequence models call its direction correctly 82% of the time at 0.1 s, 71–72% at 1 s and 56–57% at 10 s on BTC 15m. On the BTC perp it is 65% / 57% / 52% for the GRU.

More compute keeps paying (scaling check). The same GRU trained for 60 min on 14 threads (11,777 steps, ~5 epochs) reaches test R² 0.262 / 0.164 / 0.123 / 0.018, up from 0.251 / 0.158 / 0.119 / 0.018 at 30 min. That is +13% over handcrafted LightGBM at 0.1 s and +8% at 1 s. Validation R² was still rising at the end. The GRU beats the Transformer on CPU because it runs ~3× more steps per minute at the same ~345k parameters; on a GPU that ordering may flip.

Continued Transformer. Resumed from the 75-min weights (not from scratch) for another 90 min (2,941 steps at batch 512, 30 threads). Validation R² at 0.1 s rose 0.224 → 0.244 → 0.252, and held-out test R² went from 0.233 / 0.154 / 0.116 / 0.018 to 0.244 / 0.158 / 0.119 / 0.017. That puts the Transformer level with the 30-min GRU and ahead of handcrafted LightGBM (0.232 / 0.152 / 0.114 / 0.015), still behind the 60-min GRU (0.262 / 0.164 / 0.123 / 0.018). It was still improving when the time cap hit; a full checkpoint (weights + optimiser) is saved and backed up, so it can be resumed again exactly.

Caveat for trading: these are R² on mid changes, with 76% of 0.1 s targets exactly zero. The notes already show this kind of edge is eaten by taker fees; the raw-event models make the forecast better, not the fee arithmetic.

overview_next:
Suggested next steps

  • Use the toxicity model on the maker side: widen or skew quotes when the next order looks like a touch-clearing chaser. That is where this information pays; taking does not clear two fees.
  • Scale the raw-event models on a GPU. Both were still improving when their CPU time ran out; the GRU scaling run will show the slope.
  • Test the models on tonight's fresh tape (Nov 17) for a true out-of-period check.
  • Confirm the Kalshi perp taker fee: 2 bp/side was assumed and drives every perp net-PnL number.
oos: The ranking holds on unseen days. Pooled over 20 BTC 15-minute days the models never saw, 0.1s R² is: GRU 60 min 0.262, Transformer 75+90 min 0.247, GRU 30 min 0.247, LightGBM 0.235. This almost exactly matches the original single test day.

The raw-event models usually win, not always. On BTC 15m, the 60-minute GRU beats LightGBM at 0.1s on 17 of 20 unseen days, and the continued Transformer on 14. The continued Transformer improved on its 75-minute checkpoint on most days, so the extra training generalised.

The perp result is the most robust. The perp GRU beats LightGBM on 19 of 19 unseen days, with 0.1s R² of 0.173 against 0.092. LightGBM's perp R² decays toward October (0.03–0.05 on Oct 4–6), while the GRU stays at 0.13–0.24.

No decay over 18 days, but today is harder. September and early October scores do not trend down with distance from training. On today's tape (Nov 17, 57 days later, 16 hours, 44 BTC 15m markets), every model drops to about 0.12–0.14 at 0.1s, LightGBM included. Mid moves today are larger and less often zero (std at 0.1s is 1.03 ticks, against 0.81–0.91 in September/October; P(no move) is 0.71, against 0.75–0.76). That points to a shift in the market, not a model-specific failure. The raw-event models still edge out LightGBM (GRU 0.140, LightGBM 0.122).
Perps today: GRU 0.142, LightGBM 0.078, Transformer 0.073 at 0.1s, in line with the October range.
Caveat: per-day R² swings by several points with the sample drawn. Trust the pooled numbers and day counts more than any single day.
oos_method:
• The models are the frozen checkpoints from the training runs, with no fine-tuning. Normalisation statistics are recomputed exactly as in training (same files, same seed, train days Sep 18–21).
  • LightGBM is refit with the identical recipe and early-stopped on Sep 22, so its numbers match the original baseline.
  • New days: Sep 15–17, Sep 24 – Oct 9, and Nov 17 (today, collected by kalshi-collector since 08:30 UTC). Each was extracted from the tape and tokenised with the same pipeline (extract.py → features.py … fair). The perp tape starts Sep 16, and Sep 15 BTC 15m is a partial day (5,000 samples).
  • Sampling per day: up to 500 anchors per BTC 15m market, and 15,000 perp anchors. Pooled scores are sample-weighted means of per-day R² over unseen days only. Sep 22 and Sep 23 are shown for reference but excluded from pooling.
  • Code: code/eval_fair.py, code/run_oos.sh, code/oos_summary.py. wandb run fair-out-of-sample (group fair-oos). VM time was about 55 minutes (≈ $1.70).
